questions.q: How is the marginal distribution of X obtained from a joint distribution f(x, y)?
options: By dividing f(x, y) by f(y)
By summing or integrating f(x, y) over all values of y
By multiplying f(x, y) by f(y)
By taking the maximum of f(x, y) over y
questions.explain: The marginal distribution of X is recovered by summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) the other variable out of the joint distribution: f(x) = ∫ f(x, y) dy.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between independence and zero covariance?
options: They are exactly equivalent — one implies the other
Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence
Zero covariance implies independence, but independence does not imply zero covariance
questions.explain: Independence is a strictly stronger condition: it requires the joint density to factor for every pair of values, which forces zero covariance. But variables can have zero covariance while still being dependent (e.g., a nonlinear relationship).

questions.q: Two assets have Var(X) = 0.04, Var(Y) = 0.09, and Cov(X,Y) = -0.01. What is Var(X + Y) for an equally-weighted combination (w=1 each, before scaling)?
The law of total variance states Var(X) = E[Var(X|Y)] + Var(E[X|Y]). What does the second term, Var(E[X|Y]), represent?
options: The average variance within each value of Y
The variance of the conditional means themselves, as Y varies — i.e., between-group variance
The covariance between X and Y
Always zero, regardless of the data
questions.explain: Var(E[X|Y]) is the variance of the conditional expectation across different values of Y — how much the conditional means themselves differ from each other, i.e. the between-group component of total variance.

questions.q: What correlation value would two random variables have if Cov(X,Y) = 0.006, σₓ = 0.12, and σᵥ = 0.05?
questions.explain: ρ(X,Y) = Cov(X,Y) / (σₓ σᵥ) = 0.006 / (0.12 × 0.05) = 0.006 / 0.006 = 1.0 — correlation is exactly 1 here.
